(CNN) -- Massachusetts sued the U.S. government on Wednesday, challenging the constitutionality of a federal law that defines marriage as the union of a man and a woman. The state of Massachusetts says the Defense of Marriage Act denies same-sex couples essential rights. "We're taking this action today because, first, we believe that [the Defense of Marriage Act] directly interferes with Massachusetts' long-standing sovereign authority to define and regulate the marital status of its residents," Attorney General Martha Coakley said Wednesday afternoon. "Massachusetts has a single category of married persons, and we view all married persons equally and identically," she said. "DOMA divides that category into two distinct and unequal classes of marriage." The lawsuit argues that the act, which became law in 1996, denies same-sex couples essential rights and protections, including federal income tax credits, employment and retirement benefits, health insurance coverage and Social Security payments. "In enacting DOMA, Congress overstepped its authority, undermined states' efforts to recognize marriages between same-sex couples, and codified an animus towards gay and lesbian people," the state wrote in the lawsuit, which was filed Wednesday in federal court. Massachusetts, the first state to legalize gay marriage, said that about 16,000 same-sex couples have been married there since 2004, when it began issuing marriage licenses. Since that time, the lawsuit said, "the security and stability of families has been strengthened in important ways throughout the state. " The state is challenging Section 3 of the law, which defines marriage as "a legal union between one man and one woman as husband and wife" and a spouse as "a person of the opposite sex who is a husband or a wife." Before the act, the lawsuit argues, defining marital status was the prerogative of the states. The law "eviscerated more than 200 years of federal government deference to the states with respect to defining marriage," it said. The lawsuit also argues that the law forces Massachusetts to treat same-sex married couples differently from heterosexual married couples, particularly through determining who qualifies for the state's Medicaid program, known as MassHealth, and whether a same-sex spouse of a veteran can be buried in a veteran cemetery. "But for DOMA, married individuals in same-sex relationships in the commonwealth would receive the same status, obligations, responsibilities, rights, and protections as married individuals in different-sex relationships under local, state, and federal laws," the lawsuit said. The defendants named in the lawsuit include the Department of Health and Human Services, Secretary of Health and Human Services Kathleen Sebelius, the Department of Veterans Affairs, Veterans Affairs Secretary Eric Shinseki and the United States itself. Charles Miller, a spokesman for the Department of Justice, said the department will review the case but noted that President Obama supports the legislative repeal of the Defense of Marriage Act. In March, Gay & Lesbian Advocates & Defenders -- the same Boston-based group that successfully argued in 2003 for same-sex marriage rights in Massachusetts -- also sued the federal government over Section 3 of the Defense of Marriage Act. Besides Massachusetts, three other states recognize same-sex marriages: Connecticut, Maine, and Iowa. Vermont and New Hampshire will join their company when same-sex marriages become legal later this year and early next year.

On Wednesday, Massachusetts made a significant legal move by filing a lawsuit against the United States government, directly challenging the constitutionality of the Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA). This action places the state at the forefront of the national debate over marriage equality and federal authority.

## The Legal Argument

Attorney General Martha Coakley, who is leading the charge on behalf of the Commonwealth, has laid out a compelling constitutional argument against the federal statute. According to Coakley, DOMA fundamentally interferes with Massachusetts' sovereign authority to define and regulate marital status within its own borders. The lawsuit contends that by refusing to recognize same-sex marriages that are legally performed and recognized under state law, the federal government has effectively created two distinct and unequal classes of marriage—one that receives full federal recognition and another that does not, despite both being equally valid under state law.

## Tangible Harms to Same-Sex Couples

The lawsuit goes beyond abstract constitutional principles to detail the concrete, everyday harms that DOMA inflicts on same-sex married couples in Massachusetts. Because the federal government does not recognize these marriages, affected couples are denied access to a wide range of essential rights and protections that opposite-sex married couples take for granted. These include:

- **Tax benefits**, such as the ability to file joint federal tax returns and claim marital tax credits
- **Employment and retirement benefits**, including spousal coverage under federal employee benefit programs
- **Health insurance protections** that would otherwise extend to a legally married spouse
- **Social Security payments**, including spousal and survivor benefits that are automatically available to heterosexual married couples

By denying these protections, the lawsuit argues, DOMA imposes real financial and practical burdens on families who are otherwise treated as fully married under Massachusetts law.

## Targeting Section 3 of DOMA

# Massachusetts Sues Federal Government Over Defense of Marriage Act

**BOSTON** — Massachusetts Attorney General Martha Coakley announced Wednesday that the Commonwealth has filed a federal lawsuit challenging the constitutionality of the Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA), arguing the 1996 law unlawfully discriminates against same-sex couples legally married under state law and infringes on states' rights to define marriage.

The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court in Boston, contends that DOMA violates the Tenth Amendment by intruding on a policy area traditionally reserved for states, while also denying federal benefits to legally married same-sex couples in Massachusetts, where such marriages have been legal since 2004.

"This is really a case about the Commonwealth's sovereign authority to determine who's married," Coakley said at a press conference announcing the suit. "The federal government, through DOMA, is discriminating against a certain class of married individuals here in Massachusetts, and it's doing so without justification."

The suit specifically targets Section 3 of DOMA, which defines marriage for federal purposes as strictly between one man and one woman. As a result, same-sex couples legally married in Massachusetts are barred from receiving a host of federal benefits — including joint tax filing, Social Security survivor benefits, and health insurance coverage for spouses of federal and state employees who participate in federally funded programs.

Coakley argued that the law forces Massachusetts to treat its own citizens unequally in order to comply with federal mandates. "Massachusetts is being required, in effect, to discriminate against its own citizens in order to receive federal funding," she said. "We don't think that's constitutional, and we don't think Congress had the authority to pass this kind of legislation that so clearly infringes on a state's right to regulate marriage."

The lawsuit comes amid a broader national debate over same-sex marriage rights, with several other states and advocacy organizations pursuing separate legal challenges to DOMA. Legal scholars say the Massachusetts case is notable because it approaches the issue from a states' rights angle rather than solely through equal protection arguments, potentially appealing to a broader ideological coalition.

Coakley emphasized that the suit is not asking the federal government to require other states to recognize same-sex marriages, but rather to stop penalizing Massachusetts for choices made within its own borders.

"We're not suing to force anyone to change their own marriage laws," Coakley said. "We're simply saying that once a marriage is legal in Massachusetts, the federal government cannot come in and say, 'We don't recognize that marriage for these purposes.' That's not right, and we believe it's not constitutional."

The Department of Justice has not yet issued a formal response to the lawsuit. Legal experts anticipate the case could take months, if not years, to work through the courts, with the possibility of eventually reaching the U.S. Supreme Court given the constitutional questions at stake.

Reaction to the announcement was swift, with LGBT advocacy groups praising the move as a significant step forward, while some conservative organizations criticized it as government overreach into a matter they argue should remain under federal jurisdiction to ensure uniformity across states.

For now, Coakley said her office is focused on the legal arguments ahead. "This is about fairness, this is about equal treatment under the law, and this is about respecting the Commonwealth's right to make its own decisions about marriage," she said. "We look forward to making our case in court."

*CNN will continue to follow developments in this case as it proceeds through the federal court system.*

## Massachusetts Challenges the Defense of Marriage Act (2009)

**BOSTON** — In July 2009, Massachusetts Attorney General Martha Coakley filed a federal lawsuit against the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, challenging the constitutionality of the Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA), marking a significant moment in the legal fight over marriage equality.

### The Legal Basis for the Suit

The lawsuit centered on Section 3 of DOMA, the 1996 federal law that defined marriage as between one man and one woman for purposes of federal law. Massachusetts argued this provision:

- **Violated the Tenth Amendment** by intruding on the state's historical authority to define and regulate marriage
- **Denied federal benefits** to legally married same-sex couples in Massachusetts, including access to joint tax filing, Social Security survivor benefits, and the ability to bury spouses in veterans' cemeteries
- **Forced the state to discriminate** in administering federal-state programs, since Massachusetts had to treat its own legally married same-sex couples differently than opposite-sex couples when distributing federal funds

### Historical Background

Massachusetts became the first state to legalize same-sex marriage following the Supreme Judicial Court's landmark 2003 decision in *Goodridge v. Department of Public Health*, which found that denying marriage licenses to same-sex couples violated the state constitution. Same-sex marriages began in Massachusetts in May 2004.

However, DOMA—signed by President Bill Clinton in 1996—meant that even as Massachusetts recognized these marriages, the federal government did not. This created a two-tiered system where couples were married under state law but legal strangers under federal law.

### The Coakley Argument

Attorney General Coakley's suit made a novel federalism argument, contending that:

> Marriage regulation had traditionally been left to individual states, and the federal government's intervention through DOMA represented federal overreach into an area of traditional state sovereignty.

This states' rights framing was notable because it drew from conservative legal principles typically used in other contexts, applying them to advance marriage equality.

### Legal Outcome

In July 2010, U.S. District Judge Joseph Tauro ruled in favor of Massachusetts, finding that DOMA violated the Tenth Amendment and the Spending Clause. This victory was later effectively affirmed when the Supreme Court struck down Section 3 of DOMA in *United States v. Windsor* (2013), a case that similarly found the federal government's refusal to recognize state-sanctioned same-sex marriages unconstitutional.

---

## Broader Significance

This case was part of a series of legal challenges that ultimately led to *Obergefell v. Hodges* (2015), in which the Supreme Court ruled that same-sex marriage bans nationwide were unconstitutional, legalizing same-sex marriage across all fifty states.

---

# Commonwealth of Massachusetts v. U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (2009)

## Overview

On July 8, 2009, the Commonwealth of Massachusetts filed a lawsuit against the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) challenging the constitutionality of Section 3 of the Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA). This case was significant as the first instance of a state government directly suing the federal government over DOMA's constitutionality, rather than individual plaintiffs bringing suit.

## Background on DOMA

The Defense of Marriage Act was signed into law by President Bill Clinton in September 1996. It contained two key provisions:

- **Section 2**: Allowed states to refuse recognition of same-sex marriages performed in other states
- **Section 3**: Defined marriage, for federal purposes, as a union between one man and one woman, thereby denying federal recognition and benefits to same-sex couples even when legally married under state law

## Massachusetts' Legal Position

Massachusetts argued that Section 3 of DOMA:

1. **Violated the Tenth Amendment** by interfering with the state's traditional authority to define and regulate marriage
2. **Violated the Spending Clause** by forcing Massachusetts to discriminate against its own legally married same-sex couples in order to receive federal funding for certain programs (such as veterans' cemeteries and Medicaid)
3. **Violated equal protection principles** embedded in the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause

The Commonwealth contended that DOMA created a two-tiered marriage system within the state, where legally married same-sex couples were denied over 1,000 federal benefits and protections available to opposite-sex married couples, including tax benefits, Social Security survivor benefits, and immigration sponsorship rights.

## Background: Same-Sex Marriage Recognition by States

At the time of the lawsuit, Massachusetts held a unique position in this legal landscape:

- **Massachusetts (2004)**: Became the first U.S. state to legalize same-sex marriage following the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court's decision in *Goodridge v. Department of Public Health* (2003)
- **Connecticut (2008)**: Legalized same-sex marriage via judicial ruling in *Kerrigan v. Commissioner of Public Health*
- **Iowa (2009)**: The Iowa Supreme Court legalized same-sex marriage in *Varnum v. Brien* (April 2009)
- **Vermont (2009)**: Became the first state to legalize same-sex marriage through legislative action (April 2009), overriding a gubernatorial veto
- **Maine (2009)**: The legislature approved same-sex marriage in May 2009, though this was later suspended pending a referendum (voters would ultimately reject it in November 2009, before approving it in 2012)
- **New Hampshire (2009)**: Legalized same-sex marriage through legislation signed in June 2009, effective January 2010

This wave of state-level recognition created increasing friction with federal law, as more legally married same-sex couples faced denial of federal benefits despite their marriages being fully valid under state law.

## Related Litigation

Massachusetts' lawsuit proceeded alongside a related case, *Gill v. Office of Personnel Management*, filed by GLAD (Gay & Lesbian Advocates & Defenders) on behalf of individual same-sex couples and widowers in Massachusetts who were denied federal benefits. Both cases were assigned to Judge Joseph Tauro of the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts and were argued together.

## Outcome

On July 8, 2010, Judge Tauro ruled in favor of Massachusetts, finding Section 3 of DOMA unconstitutional on both Tenth Amendment and Spending Clause grounds. This ruling, combined with the *Gill* decision (which found DOMA violated equal protection principles), was appealed by the federal government to the First Circuit Court of Appeals, which upheld the lower court's rulings in 2012.

## Historical Significance

This litigation was part of a broader legal strategy that ultimately contributed to the Supreme Court's landmark decision in *United States v. Windsor* (2013), which struck down Section 3 of DOMA as unconstitutional, marking a pivotal moment in the legal recognition of same-sex marriage in the United States. This case, alongside *Windsor*, laid important groundwork for the Supreme Court's subsequent 2015 decision in *Obergefell v. Hodges*, which established a constitutional right to same-sex marriage nationwide.
